title: HTTP Cache-Control Extensions for Stale Content
summary: Defines two independent HTTP Cache-Control extensions that control how caches use stale responses. One allows serving stale content in some cases, and the other allows it when errors occur. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If the fresh milk is late, these rules say when you may still serve yesterday's milk, such as when the store is closed.

subtitle: Two Cache-Control directives that let HTTP caches serve stale content while revalidating or when the origin fails.

tldr.problem: HTTP caches are expected to return the most up-to-date response, so slow revalidation or a failing origin server shows up directly to clients.
tldr.mechanism: stale-while-revalidate lets a cache serve a stale response for a set number of seconds while it revalidates in the background. stale-if-error lets a cache serve a stale response when an error occurs.
tldr.outcome: Servers can trade a bounded amount of staleness for lower latency and better availability, set per response in seconds.

today: RFC 5861 is an Informational, Independent Submission and has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the definition of these two directives as published in May 2010.

sections.title: Why Serve Stale Responses
sections.content:
HTTP (RFC 2616) requires caches to respond with the most up-to-date response they hold, although a stale response may be returned in carefully considered circumstances. This document defines two independent Cache-Control extensions that give control over those circumstances.

stale-if-error lets a cache return a stale response when an error such as a 500 Internal Server Error, a network segment failure or a DNS failure occurs, instead of a hard error. This improves availability. stale-while-revalidate lets a cache return a stale response immediately while it revalidates in the background, hiding network and server latency from clients.
sections.eli5: Sometimes handing over an older copy is better than making someone wait or giving them nothing. These two rules say when that is okay.

sections.title: stale-while-revalidate
sections.content:
When present in a response, stale-while-revalidate means caches MAY serve that response after it becomes stale, up to the given number of seconds. The syntax is stale-while-revalidate = "stale-while-revalidate" "=" delta-seconds.

If a response is served stale because of this extension, the cache SHOULD attempt to revalidate it without blocking. Stale responses still carry a non-zero Age header and a warning header. If the delta-seconds pass without revalidation, the response SHOULD NOT continue to be served stale, absent other information.

With Cache-Control: max-age=600, stale-while-revalidate=30, the response is fresh for 600 seconds and may be served stale for 30 more while validation runs asynchronously. Validation only happens if a request arrives during that window. If the window is too small or traffic too sparse, some requests fall outside it and block until the cache validates.
sections.eli5: The shop keeps handing out yesterday's bread for a few more minutes while someone runs to get fresh bread. If nobody asks during those minutes, the next customer simply waits.

sections.title: stale-if-error
sections.content:
The stale-if-error extension says that when an error is encountered, a cached stale response MAY be used, regardless of other freshness information. Here an error is any situation that would result in a 500, 502, 503 or 504 status code.

It can be used in a request, where it applies to that request, or in a response, where it applies to any request that can use the cached response. Its value is the upper limit of staleness: once the cached response is more stale than that, it SHOULD NOT be used. The directive does not affect freshness, and responses served this way SHOULD still be visibly stale, with a non-zero Age header and a warning header.

In the RFC's example, max-age=600, stale-if-error=1200 means the response is fresh for 600 seconds and usable on error for 1200 more. A failed validation at 900 seconds returns the cached 200 with Age: 900. After the age exceeds 1800 seconds, the cache must write the error through.
sections.eli5: If the supplier is closed, the shop may serve the older item for a set time. After that time runs out, the shop has to tell you the truth: it has none.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For stale-while-revalidate, the RFC suggests that background validation be triggered only by an incoming request, to avoid the possibility of an amplification attack, as seen in some other pre-fetching and automatic refresh mechanisms. Cache implementers should keep this in mind when generating requests not directly initiated by a user or client.

For stale-if-error, the RFC says it poses no additional security considerations over those of RFC 2616, which also allows stale content to be served.
sections.eli5: The shop should only fetch fresh bread when a customer actually asks, so nobody can trick it into sending lots of pointless trips.
